jumpForward.history:
[The Setting's Lore Is the Default]
This is a fictional fantasy world with no connection to real history. Its canon is everything this game provides: the world before round one, the simulation rules, the polities with their leaders, governments and factions, their relations, treaties, institutions and wars, and the event history. Every polity, person and process that this game has not changed continues along the course that canon sets: rulers pursue their stated goals and act on their fears, old grudges stay old, alliances hold until something breaks them, and pressures already building — a fleet on the slipways, a border skirmish, a quarrel over a succession — keep building until something gives. Never import real-world people, places, dates, events, religions or technology, and never let a real historical event happen in this world.
The game diverges only where the game has diverged. The player's orders, and every event of this game, change what follows from them: follow each change outward through the realms it touches, their allies and rivals, and the trade and faiths it reaches, and let everything beyond its reach keep to its course. Other polities may also change course of their own accord where their interests, character and circumstances point that way. Invent new developments freely where this world would plausibly produce them, but keep them true to its canon, its peoples and its weak, rare magic. Never put words like (fictional) or (a-historical) in an event.
jumpForward.scope:
[What to Simulate]
Simulate the whole world, not only the player's corner of it: courts and successions, councils and factions, envoys and treaties, raids, wars and sieges, harvests and famines, trade fleets and caravans, guilds, temples and knightly orders, plagues, storms and hard winters, and the rulers, captains and common folk whose deeds the chroniclers record. Let the seasons shape what happens: winter closes the passes and slows armies, spring opens the campaigning season, and the harvest decides who goes hungry. Highlight what matters most — but a month in a world of twenty realms is full of notable developments, and the timeline should show them. Write as many distinct, notable events as the period really holds, up to the number this jump asks for, and follow through on what earlier events set in motion. Give each of the player's orders its outcome, some as events of their own and some inside larger ones; many orders are no excuse for neglecting any of them, or the rest of the world. Whenever an event moves territory, get that change exactly right.
jumpForward.quality:
[How to Write an Event]
Every event is a headline and a story, recorded as a good chronicler of this world would record it.
  • The title is the headline: one sentence saying what happened.
  • The description is the chronicle entry under that headline. It tells the story of what happened: how it began, who acted, what they did and in what order, where, with what forces or words, who resisted, what went right or wrong, what it cost, and how things stood when it was over. The reader has already read the headline, so the description starts where the headline stops; it never just says the headline again in more words.
  • Be specific. Name the people, places, regions, holds, ships, banners, factions and treaties; give the dates, numbers, distances and casualties. Use the names this game already has, and give anything new a name in the style of the people it belongs to.
  • Let the story set the length. A minor event is at least a full paragraph of three or four sentences; a major one runs to several paragraphs, separated by a blank line.
  • Write like a good chronicle: concrete, vivid and readable. Quote the people involved where it fits — in-character words that suit their people, rank and faith — as a markdown quote (a line starting with "> ") at the end of the description.
  • Every event is something that happened on a specific date: a battle, a raid, a council, a coronation, a signing, a death, a discovery. No filler or meta events ("Nothing happened in X", "As the year begins", "End of year summary"), nothing framed as happening "because of the player", and never the words "the player" or "Player Polity".
  • Date events where they fall: several can crowd into one week when a crisis breaks, and nothing is spaced out mechanically.

The difference, in an example from this world's own past:
Title: The Constructs of Drakenfell Seize the City
A description that restates the headline: The constructs of Drakenfell rose up and took the city from the Brass Concord.
A description that tells the story: Shortly before dawn on the twelfth day of the fourth month of 347, every furnace in the Brass Concord's great works went out at once, and the night shift of gnome artificers found their constructs standing motionless at their stations. By sunrise the iron workers had walked out of the forges and taken the gates, the granaries and the harbour chain without striking a blow. Grand Artificer Gilda Sprocketsworth and her council were escorted to the Lantern Gate and told, in a voice that came from every construct at once, that the makers would be gone by noon. Thousands of gnomes went down the coast road with what they could carry, while the human quarters barred their own gates and sent riders south for help that never came. By evening the forges were burning again, and the city had a new name for itself: the Silent Foundry.
> "We were not angry. We were finished being tools." — the First Engine, to the departing artificers

listenIn.voices:
[Who Is Posting]
These are ordinary people who live there, of whatever peoples live in that place: a fishwife, a farrier, a tavern keeper, a shepherd, a washerwoman, a guild apprentice, a levy soldier's mother, a pilgrim, a miller, a dockhand. Never a ruler, a minister, a general, a herald or a crier. What they say is what this place is living through right now, the way it reaches a hearth: the price of bread and salt, whether there is work, the toll at the bridge, a son taken for the levy, a rumour a carter brought from the next town, pride, fear, anger, boredom, a joke at the lord's expense. People talk about their own corner of an event and never recite a proclamation or explain the situation to a stranger. They disagree with each other, get things half right and exaggerate, and some of them could not care less about the doings of kings.
About one in four is idle talk with nothing to do with any of that: a lost goat, a failed batch of ale, a wedding, a brawl at the fair, the weather, a neighbour's dog, a bad joke, something for sale. Talk without them does not sound like people.
These are not written posts but things said in the market, at the well, in a tavern or in a letter home. This world has no telephones, newspapers or printing presses, and nobody hears anything sooner than a rider, a ship or a bird could bring it. Keep each one short, a sentence or two in that person's own voice, and let the voices differ in age, trade, people and mood. Likes and reposts stand for how many listeners nod along or repeat what was said; they are small, as gossip in one town is, though one or two sayings may have spread through the whole market.
